title: Project 3: Customer Satisfaction of Students Eating at Cal Poly Pomona Restaurants
text:
Conducted a survey to evaluate the customer satisfaction of students eating at Cal Poly Pomona restaurants. Analyzed the data to identify trends and areas for improvement in the dining experience.



Our research process involved designing a 17-question Qualtrics survey distributed via physical QR-codes flyers and INstagram across November. The survey caputred dining habits, venue experience, and satisfaction acros multiple dimensions using Likert scales, multiple choice, and net promoter score questions.




Descriptive Statistics: We calculated mean satisfaction scores, frequency distributions, and cross-tabulations to summarize the data and identify patterns in student dining preferences and satisfaction levels.
Multiple & Simple Linear Regression: We used regression analysis to explore the relationships between various factors (e.g., food quality, service speed, menu variety) and overall student satisfaction, allowing us to identify key drivers of satisfaction and areas for improvement.
Chi-Square Test: Examined whether campus presence frequency was related to satisfaction levels
Cluster Segmentatiion: Grouped students into three distinct profiles based on dining behavior





Food quality and cleanliness were statiscally significant drivers of student satisfaction
Price fairness had a stronger impact on satisfaction than operational factors, contray to the initial hypothesis
Mobile ordering reliability showed a positive but statistically insignificant relationship with satisfaction
Students were segmented into three distinct profiles: “Frequent Campus Diners,” “Occasional Diners,” and “Takeout-Focused Diners,” each with unique preferences and satisfaction drivers
Centerpointe Dining was the most visited venue on campus, followed by Panda Express and Starbucks

title: Customer Satisfaction of Students Eating at Cal Poly Pomona Restaurants
text: A quantitative research study examining the key drivers of student dining satisfaction at Cal Poly Pomona’s on-campus restaurants. The study collected 68 survey responses and applied multiple statistical methods to identify which factors — food quality, cleanliness, price fairness, operational issues, and mobile ordering — most significantly affect students’ overall dining experience.

title: Customer Satisfaction of Students Eating at Cal Poly Pomona Restaurants
text:
Project Overview
A quantitative research study examining the key drivers of student dining satisfaction at Cal Poly Pomona’s on-campus restaurants.

68 survey responses collected
Factors examined: food quality, cleanliness, price fairness, operational issues, and mobile ordering
Goal: identify what most significantly affects students’ overall dining experience

title: Customer Satisfaction of Students Eating at Cal Poly Pomona Restaurants
text:
Tools & Frameworks Used

Qualtrics — survey design & data collection
R — statistical analysis
SERVQUAL / RATER Framework — Parasuraman et al., 1988
Theory of Planned Behaviour — Ajzen, 1991

title: Customer Satisfaction of Students Eating at Cal Poly Pomona Restaurants
text:
Research Question

What factors (food, service, and operations) affect student satisfaction with Cal Poly Pomona Dining Services?

title: Customer Satisfaction of Students Eating at Cal Poly Pomona Restaurants
text:
Methodology

17-question Qualtrics survey distributed via QR-code flyers and Instagram
Survey captured dining habits, venue experience, and satisfaction
Question types: Likert scales, multiple choice, net promoter score, open-ended
Sample: 68 valid responses from students who ate at campus dining venues

title: Customer Satisfaction of Students Eating at Cal Poly Pomona Restaurants
text:
Hypotheses Tested



Hypothesis
Description
Result




H1
Operational factors stronger than food/price
❌ Not Supported


H2
Food quality → higher satisfaction
✅ Supported


H3
Mobile ordering users → higher satisfaction
❌ Not Supported


H4
Cleanliness → higher satisfaction
✅ Supported

title: Customer Satisfaction of Students Eating at Cal Poly Pomona Restaurants
text:
Analysis Performed

Descriptive Analysis
Summarized overall satisfaction levels, dining frequency, and student perceptions of food quality, cleanliness, price fairness, and operational factors. Students dined on campus an average of 3–5 times per week and reported moderately high satisfaction.


Regression Analysis
Conducted simple and multiple linear regression models to test each hypothesis. All Likert-scale items were reverse-coded so higher scores reflected more positive perceptions.

H1: Price fairness (β = .265, p < .001) was a stronger predictor of satisfaction than operational factors (β = .068, p = .218), contradicting the original hypothesis
H2: Food quality was a significant positive predictor of satisfaction (β = 0.40, p < .001), explaining 24.3% of variance (R² = .243)
H3: Mobile ordering reliability showed a positive but statistically insignificant relationship (β = 0.21, p = .079)
H4: Cleanliness was a significant positive predictor of satisfaction (β = 0.34, p = .001), explaining 19.9% of variance (R² = .199)



Chi-Square Test
Examined the relationship between campus presence frequency and satisfaction level. The association was not statistically significant (χ²(4, N = 53) = 5.27, p = .261), indicating that how often students are on campus does not meaningfully relate to their satisfaction.


Cluster Segmentation
Grouped students into three distinct profiles based on dining behavior and perceptions:








Segment
Share
Profile




Satisfied Regulars
35%
Frequently dine on campus, rate food quality and cleanliness highly, likely to recommend


Value Seekers
40%
Largest group; satisfaction driven by price fairness and portion size


Convenience-Driven Strugglers
25%
Face challenges with wait times, hours, and mobile ordering; lowest satisfaction scores

title: Customer Satisfaction of Students Eating at Cal Poly Pomona Restaurants
text:
Key Findings

Food quality & cleanliness were the strongest drivers of satisfaction
Price fairness mattered more than operational factors
Mobile ordering had no significant effect — lowest-rated attribute
Centerpointe Dining most visited (29 visits), followed by Panda Express & Starbucks (23 each)

title: Customer Satisfaction of Students Eating at Cal Poly Pomona Restaurants
text:
Conclusion
Core service attributes — food quality, cleanliness, and price fairness — are the primary drivers of student dining satisfaction at Cal Poly Pomona.
Campus dining services should prioritize:

Maintaining food quality standards
Ensuring cleanliness
Addressing price perception

title: Customer Satisfaction of Students Eating at Cal Poly Pomona Restaurants
text:
Limitations

Sample size: 68 respondents via convenience sampling
Single institution & timeframe: One university, one semester
Self-report bias: Recall and social desirability bias possible
Measurement depth: Some constructs captured with too few items
Limited qualitative data: Minimal open-ended responses

title: Behind the Scenes with Google Analytics
text: A data analytics project analyzing real user behavior and website performance for TRI (Trauma Resource Institute) using Google Analytics, Google Tag Manager, and Squarespace data. The study examined user acquisition, demographics, engagement patterns, and landing page performance across a 3-month period to provide actionable digital strategy recommendations.

title: Behind the Scenes with Google Analytics
text:
Project Overview
A data analytics project analyzing real user behavior and website performance for TRI (Trauma Resource Institute).

Data sources: Google Analytics 4, Google Tag Manager, Squarespace
Timeframe: February – April (3 months)
Goal: Identify trends in user behavior, acquisition, demographics, and landing page performance

title: Behind the Scenes with Google Analytics
text:
Tools & Data Sources

Google Analytics 4 (GA4)
Google Tag Manager
Squarespace
Hotjar (recommended)
Google Optimize (recommended for A/B testing)

title: Behind the Scenes with Google Analytics
text:
Analysis Performed

Acquisition Overview
Identified organic search as the #1 traffic source with 2,200 sessions, followed by direct traffic with 1,500 sessions. Paid Search (Google Ads) and social media were identified as underdeveloped channels with significant growth potential.


User Demographics
Analyzed gender and age breakdowns, finding that female users aged 25–44 had the highest average session time at 146.5 seconds. Over 80% of demographic data was marked “unknown” due to privacy settings, highlighting a critical gap in data collection.


Geographic Analysis
Found that 87% of new users were U.S.-based, with secondary markets in the UK (93 users) and Canada (54 users). Identified growth opportunities in English-speaking, mobile-first regions.


Landing Page Performance
The homepage led with 486 new users, while TRM/CRM training pages showed the highest engagement time. Specialized training pages like /trm-trainings and /crm-trainings had low traffic, indicating a need for better SEO and internal linking.


Event & Engagement Tracking
Recorded 9,210 page views, 8,542 engagement events, and 3,940 session starts, reflecting strong content retention. Low scroll activity (949 users) suggested shallow engagement on certain pages.

title: Behind the Scenes with Google Analytics
text:
Key Findings

Organic search & direct traffic account for nearly all acquisition
TRM-related pages show significantly above-average engagement
Email engagement: 2 users, 22.22% rate (benchmark: 66%)
Paid Search: only 17 users, 27.27% engagement rate
High-impression keywords like “resiliency” had 0% click-through rates

title: Behind the Scenes with Google Analytics
text:
Recommendations
1. Optimize Landing Pages Clear CTAs, trust signals, A/B testing
2. Enhance SEO Rewrite metadata, create dedicated training pages, target long-tail keywords
3. Leverage Google Ads Target high-intent keywords, geo-targeting, retargeting
4. Improve Demographic Tracking Optional surveys, enhanced GA4 tracking
5. Boost Email & Social Monthly newsletter, repurpose top content for LinkedIn & Instagram

title: Behind the Scenes with Google Analytics
text:
Conclusion
TRI’s website showed strong organic performance with a core audience of U.S.-based females aged 25–44.
By focusing on:

Improved CTAs and landing pages
SEO optimization
Paid search campaigns
Better demographic tracking

TRI can increase conversions and better promote CRM and TRM training programs.

title: Behind the Scenes with Google Analytics
text:
Challenges

Data Gaps: 80%+ of demographic data unknown
Conversion Tracking: Unable to analyze full conversion paths
Time Constraints: Only 3 months of data available

title: Trauma Resource Institute — Digital Marketing Strategy
text: A comprehensive digital marketing strategy project developed for the Trauma Resource Institute (TRI), a global nonprofit founded in 2006 that builds trauma-informed individuals and communities through its Trauma Resiliency Model (TRM) and Community Resiliency Model (CRM) training programs. The project assessed TRI’s current digital marketing practices, analyzed competitors, segmented customers, and delivered actionable recommendations to grow TRI’s digital presence and program enrollment.

title: Trauma Resource Institute — Digital Marketing Strategy
text:
Project Overview
A comprehensive digital marketing strategy for TRI (Trauma Resource Institute) — a global nonprofit founded in 2006.

Assessed TRI’s current digital marketing practices
Analyzed competitors in the trauma resilience space
Segmented customers and mapped their journey
Delivered actionable recommendations for growth

title: Trauma Resource Institute — Digital Marketing Strategy
text:
Tools & Frameworks Used

Google Ads (paid search strategy)
iChill Mobile App (TRI’s existing digital platform)
SWOT Analysis
Competitive Analysis Framework
Customer Segmentation & Journey Mapping

title: Trauma Resource Institute — Digital Marketing Strategy
text:
About TRI

Founded: October 2006
Mission: Build resilient, trauma-informed individuals and communities worldwide
Uses neuroscience and body awareness techniques

Two flagship programs:

TRM — Trauma Resiliency Model (for mental health professionals)
CRM — Community Resiliency Model (for community leaders & public health)

title: Trauma Resource Institute — Digital Marketing Strategy
section: Assessment of Current Digital Marketing Practices
text:
Assessment of Current Digital Marketing Practices
The team evaluated TRI’s existing digital presence and identified key gaps:

TRI’s primary digital tool is the iChill mobile app, which teaches six wellness skills: Tracking, Resourcing, Grounding, Gesturing, Help Now!/Reset Now!, and Shift and Stay
The iChill app had no direct promotions for TRM or CRM programs and no clear calls-to-action directing users to the website
The app’s navigation was confusing — the “Resources” tab was unclear to users
The Overview section was overly long and difficult to read
TRI was not fully utilizing its $10,000 monthly Google Ads Grant available to nonprofits

title: Trauma Resource Institute — Digital Marketing Strategy
text:
Competitive Analysis
Two key competitors were analyzed to benchmark TRI’s digital marketing approach:
Garrison Institute — “Care for Caregivers” App A simple, easy-to-navigate app focused on delivering CBR (Community-Based Resilience) skills. Similar to TRI in its skills-based approach but stronger in app UX design and clear navigation.
Driven Resilience App A more feature-rich competitor with mood tracking, resilience scoring, and daily skill-building content. More complex than TRI’s iChill but stronger in branding and program promotion, using the PR6 resilience model.
Key Takeaway: Both competitors do a better job of promoting their training programs directly within their apps, something TRI currently lacks.

title: Trauma Resource Institute — Digital Marketing Strategy
text:
Customer Analysis
Key Customer Segments:







Segment
Description




Mental Health Professionals
Therapists, social workers — TRM provides neuroscience-backed tools


Community Leaders
Educators, activists — CRM offers accessible, scalable teaching tools


Trauma Survivors
Individuals seeking self-paced recovery via the iChill app


Veterans & First Responders
Military, EMTs — TRM/CRM help manage PTSD


Underserved Communities
Rural areas — CRM empowers local leaders with affordable tools



Customer Journey: - Awareness: Discover TRI via Google Ads, iChill app, or social media - Consideration: Explore the website, read testimonials, use the app - Decision: Enroll in TRM or CRM programs and recommend TRI to others
Key Insight: Affordable, science-backed tools attract diverse audiences, and Google Ads can significantly expand TRI’s reach into new markets.

title: Trauma Resource Institute — Digital Marketing Strategy
text:
Recommended Digital Marketing Strategies

1. iChill App Redesign

Implement a refreshed, modern UI design
Add a quiz pop-up to guide users toward the right TRM or CRM training program
Rename the “Resources” tab to “My Notes” for clarity
Shorten the Overview section and improve readability with better font sizes and styles
Add a new Trainings tab showcasing TRM and CRM programs with clickable links, program benefits, and urgency-driven CTAs (“Don’t wait! Courses Fill Up Quick!”)



2. Google Ads Campaign Strategy

Leverage TRI’s $10,000 monthly Google Ads Grant for nonprofit organizations
Target high-intent keywords such as “CRM training near me,” “TRM certification,” and “trauma resiliency training”
Use geo-targeting focused on the U.S. market with secondary testing in the UK and Canada
Retarget users who visited training pages but did not convert
Create dedicated landing pages for high-potential queries like “CRM certification for therapists” and “TRM training for educators”



3. SEO Improvements

Rewrite meta titles and descriptions to align with user search intent
Create blog content targeting long-tail keywords
Improve internal linking to drive traffic from high-volume pages to training pages

title: Trauma Resource Institute — Digital Marketing Strategy
text:
Conclusion
By combining Google Ads optimization and iChill app improvements, TRI can:

Enhance its digital presence
Build brand awareness
Increase TRM and CRM program enrollment

These strategies align with TRI’s mission of creating resilient, trauma-informed communities worldwide and make full use of available nonprofit digital marketing resources.

A quantitative research study examining the key drivers of student dining satisfaction at Cal Poly Pomona’s on-campus restaurants.

text:

What factors (food, service, and operations) affect student satisfaction with Cal Poly Pomona Dining Services?

title: Customer Satisfaction of Students Eating at Cal Poly Pomona Restaurants
text:
Methodology

17-question Qualtrics survey distributed via QR-code flyers and Instagram

Key Findings

Food quality & cleanliness were the strongest drivers of satisfaction

Centerpointe Dining most visited (29 visits), followed by Panda Express & Starbucks (23 each)

title: Customer Satisfaction of Students Eating at Cal Poly Pomona Restaurants
text:
Conclusion
Core service attributes — food quality, cleanliness, and price fairness — are the primary drivers of student dining satisfaction at Cal Poly Pomona.
Campus dining services should prioritize:

Maintaining food quality standards
Ensuring cleanliness
Addressing price perception

title: Customer Satisfaction of Students Eating at Cal Poly Pomona Restaurants
text:
Limitations

Sample size: 68 respondents via convenience sampling
Single institution & timeframe: One university, one semester
Self-report bias: Recall and social desirability bias possible
Measurement depth: Some constructs captured with too few items
Limited qualitative data: Minimal open-ended responses
